newsitem.title: USA: Not guilty plea entered in spying-for-Korea case.
newsitem.headline: Not guilty plea entered in spying-for-Korea case.

text.p: A former U.S. Navy intelligence analyst entered a not guilty plea on Monday to charges of spying for his native South Korea.
Robert Kim, 57, of Sterling, Virginia, was arrested last September and indicted in March by a federal grand jury for espionage, which carries a maximum penalty of life in prison and a $250,000 fine.
U.S. District Court Judge Leonie Brinkema scheduled a hearing for May 30 on pre-trial motions by Kim's lawyers and a trial date of July 14.
Kim, who became an American citizen in 1974, worked as a civilian analyst with the Office of Naval Intelligence in Suitland, Maryland, near Washington.

In a brief hearing, the bespectacled, greying Kim wore a green Alexandria City jail jump suit, telling the judge that he may retain two new lawyers, neither of whom was believed to have criminal experience and have not been cleared to deal with top secret information involved in the case.
They would replace two court-appointed lawyers.

But after Kim said he was not sure whether he could pay for the lawyers, both of whom were out of the country this week, the judge said she would not accept any delay in the trial schedule while new lawyers prepared the case.
Prosecutors said for nine months Kim had provided a South Korean attache military information about North Korea, China and about a major U.S. computer sale to South Korea.

His daughter Leslie wrote a letter to the Washington Post saying that his only motive was "a concern for the more vulnerable country of South Korea who is against the only Stalinist country of the world. He in no way possessed a malice towards his adopted country of the United States."

But prosecutors said Kim passed classified information to South Korean navy Captain Baek Dong-Il, who was recalled by Seoul after Kim's arrest. They said he was attempting to improve his chances of doing business with South Korea.

Two other men indicted on espionage charges have pleaded guilty at the Alexandria federal courthouse. Former FBI agent Earl Edwin Pitts and ex-CIA case officer Harold James Nicholson have pleaded guilty to spying for Moscow and are scheduled to be sentenced in June.
